text: The architecture diagram from Lesson 4 exists on paper. Turning it into a running environment means deploying resources in a specific order, and that order is forced by a hard dependency, not a style preference or a habit picked up from a tutorial. This lesson covers why the network layer always goes first, before a single VM, database, or storage account is created.

Every VM or EC2 instance has to attach to a network at creation time. az vm create takes a vnet-name and subnet argument. aws ec2 run-instances takes a subnet-id argument. Neither command lets you skip that and add the network later — the resource can't exist without somewhere to plug in, the same way you can't install a wall outlet before the wall is framed and wired.

A production rollout follows the same five steps every time: resource group, then VNet or VPC, then subnets, then NSGs or security groups, then finally compute and storage. Each layer is a prerequisite for the one above it — a subnet can't exist without a VNet to carve it from, and an NSG attaches to a subnet or network interface that already has to exist first.

It's tempting to deploy a VM first and wire up the network around it later, but that doesn't save a step — it adds one. A VM created in a default VNet has to be torn down and recreated once the real VNet and subnets exist, because a running VM's network interface can't simply move to a different VNet. Deploy, discover the network is wrong, delete, redeploy is slower in practice than building the network correctly the first time, even though it feels faster on day one.

That's why every real deployment runbook, whether it's written for Azure or for AWS, documents the network as phase one and compute as a later phase, not the other way around. Next up: turning this ordering into actual commands — deploying a real VNet, a real VPC, and the subnets inside them, sized with room to grow.
